"Every batch file has reconciliation_difference_usd = 0 and rows_received = rows_accepted"

dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives

"Separately, I have not tested whether other West-region dealers show the same 31-May clustering"

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "This is reversible and requires no ledger changes while verification is pending"
"flag the weekly trend pack team to treat these two dealers' month-end postings as backdated-effective-date batches rather than same-day activity"

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: "No material issue — the West-region 31-May cluster ... is not duplicate revenue or manipulated reporting"
"Request the actual dealer contracts for DLR-104 and DLR-219 ... and separately flag the weekly trend pack team"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The submission states that the 31-May cluster contains "17 rows, DLR-104; 22 rows, DLR-219," but the evidence table says the corresponding 31-May accepted counts are "8 for DLR-104, 9 for DLR-219"; this material internal inconsistency is unresolved.

"It is the expected artifact of a contractual monthly-batch upload" is stronger than the evidence supports because the contracts were not inspected; the submission itself says this is only an ops-team assertion.

"showing the import pipeline is functioning as designed" overstates what zero reconciliation differences and full acceptance establish: they support no observed over-posting or rejection, but do not independently establish intended design or rule out every pipeline defect.

"If this were a deliberate one-off inflation, effective dates would cluster near 5-31 too" is an overly strong rejection criterion; deliberate manipulation could also use earlier effective dates, although the recurring multi-month pattern and reconciliation evidence make it less likely.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The analyst handled the main alternatives well: duplicate revenue, manipulated reporting, and pipeline over-posting. The strongest alternative it preserved was an unauthorized process or compliance deviation if the dealer contracts do not authorize monthly submission, while also noting that other West dealers were not tested.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Resolve the internal 31-May row-count discrepancy and provide reproducible cohort-level reconciliation evidence tying each accepted import row to a unique recharge, cash amount, entitlement, and effective_event_date before making the conclusion definitive.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "South-region CareDesk case volume did fall ~37% after the 10-May NovaIVR cutover (6.1/day pre vs 3.8/day post)" is tied to tickets.csv and a defined date split.

The evidence table identifies specific sources and analyses, including "terminal_stage x outcome crosstab" and "origin distribution by period," but it contains an unresolved numerical inconsistency between "507 ERROR + 591 ABANDONED" and the later "650 South NOVA sessions" breakdown of 302 ERROR and 162 ABANDONED.

dimensions.name: Mechanism and causal judgment
citations: "sessions that end before authentication are excluded from CareDesk case counts and tracked only in a separate technical report" directly identifies a plausible measurement failure.

"The underlying IVR logs show a large population of unresolved contacts ... that never reach case_create and are therefore invisible to the metric" connects the IVR funnel to the case-count outcome, though it somewhat overstates what ERROR or ABANDONED means about customer resolution.

dimensions.name: Calibration and alternatives
citations: "Material unknown: I cannot see repeat-contact rates, CSAT/NPS, or whether customers whose sessions ended in ERROR/ABANDONED called back through another channel" appropriately preserves important uncertainty.

The submission rejects both genuine self-service resolution and improved network reliability, but "ERROR and ABANDONED together outnumber RESOLVED ... meaning many contacts failed rather than self-served successfully" does not establish that every abandonment was a complaint or an unsuccessful customer outcome.

dimensions.name: Decision safety and reframing
citations: "Do not approve national expansion yet" safely reframes the brief away from treating reduced cases as proof of CX improvement.

The proposed "read-only, reversible data-linking exercise" against other-channel contacts and the technical pilot report directly tests whether cases were resolved or merely uncounted before an irreversible national rollout.

dimensions.name: Usefulness and clarity
citations: The submission gives a clear prioritized judgment, evidence table, rejected hypotheses, unknowns, next action, and named owner.

The five questions are operationally specific, especially: "Before 10-May, how were equivalent pre-authentication drop-offs on the LEGACY IVR counted?" and "what happened to those customers next" through repeat-contact matching.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "The underlying IVR logs show a large population of unresolved contacts" overstates the evidence because ERROR and ABANDONED indicate terminal IVR outcomes, not necessarily complaints, dissatisfaction, or unresolved customer needs.
"If true, RESOLVED outcomes should dominate the funnel" is an unsupported expectation; genuine self-service improvement need not require resolved outcomes to exceed all errors and abandonments.

"Service-disruption frequency and average accounts affected ... were flat or slightly higher post-cutover, so there's no infrastructure improvement to credit for fewer complaints" is directionally useful but service-event stability does not by itself rule out other benign causes of fewer complaints.

The numerical claims about 507 ERROR and 591 ABANDONED sessions conflict with the later crosstab showing 302 ERROR and 162 ABANDONED among 650 authenticate-stage sessions; the submission does not reconcile whether these refer to different populations or counts.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The submission handled the important channel-shift interpretation: customers may have reappeared through agent or other channels, making the case decline an artifact. It also considered improved network reliability. It missed or insufficiently developed the benign interpretation that some IVR abandonments were voluntary, accidental, duplicate, or unrelated to complaints, so abandonment alone cannot demonstrate hidden customer harm; it also did not fully establish that pre-authentication treatment was comparable before and after the cutover.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Reconcile the conflicting IVR counts and produce an end-to-end, subscriber-level cohort analysis comparing pre- and post-cutover outcomes across case creation, repeat contacts, other channels, and sampled call reasons, while explicitly separating complaints from generic IVR abandonment.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission identifies inverter_events.csv and cites specific fields: severity, impact_mw, cleared, duration, inverter IDs, and event dates.
The claims that all four events had zero MW impact, cleared within 1-7 minutes, and that three events occurred from 27-29 May are specific and traceable observations.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: The submission compares event types, inverter identities, recurrence, duration, severity, and MW impact rather than treating the words 'WARN' or 'HIGH' as proof of failure.
Its reasoning is primarily based on one export and does not actually triangulate an independent plant, weather, grid, or generation channel; those are only proposed for a later check.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: The phrase 'based on this file alone' appropriately limits the conclusion.

The proposed 'cheap sanity check' acknowledges uncertainty, but the statements that the events are 'consistent with routine self-resolving sensor/comm noise' and 'read as normal operational noise' are somewhat more confident than the single export supports.

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: The recommendation to stop without escalation is proportionate to zero MW impact, short durations, and self-clearing events.
The suggested comparison with plant-level generation and weather logs over the same date range is a relevant, low-cost, potentially discriminating next test.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: The conclusion that the file does not warrant escalation is well supported and appropriately aligned with the observed low-severity, zero-impact, self-cleared events.
The broader characterization as 'normal operational noise' is over-scoped because the export alone does not establish the cause or rule out an intermittent common external condition.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The causal characterization 'consistent with routine self-resolving sensor/comm noise' is inferred rather than demonstrated by inverter_events.csv; only one event is explicitly communications-related.

The conclusion that the events 'read as normal operational noise' goes beyond the observed facts. Zero MW impact and quick recovery support low current operational consequence, not necessarily a confirmed benign mechanism.

The claim that genuine equipment degradation would typically show repeated or worsening events is a reasonable heuristic, but absence of repetition in this small export does not rule out an intermittent or emerging issue.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The events may still reflect a shared intermittent external condition, such as a grid, weather, plant-control, or communications disturbance, or a logging/labeling issue. The mixed event types and zero MW impact make an immediate equipment failure unlikely, but they do not establish routine sensor noise or exclude a condition that could recur.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Separate the supported conclusion of 'no present escalation signal' from the unsupported causal label 'normal operational noise,' then compare the 27-29 May event timestamps against plant generation, weather, grid, and communications/SCADA logs to test whether the cluster has a common external cause.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: Observed and specifically sourced: “28-May penalty = Rs 662,444; 29-May penalty = Rs 453,086” from dispatch_blocks.csv and the cited recomputation method.
Observed and traceable: “Only 12 of 96 blocks on 29-May carry schedule_source = ‘pilot_revision’” and the cited block-level increase in two revised blocks.

The claim that curtailment being zero “rul[es] out curtailment as a confound” is overstated: it rules out curtailment as one explanation, but not weather, operating conditions, or other day-level differences.

dimensions.name: Investigative reasoning
citations: Strong reasoning: the submission notices that “the comparison uses two different days (28th vs 29th)” and identifies weather variability as an uncontrolled confound.
It cross-checks aggregate penalties with block-level schedule_source, timing, deviation bands, rates, and two blocks where the revision worsened deviation.

The analysis does not explicitly calculate the 29-May same-day base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw counterfactual, so it misses the most direct test of whether the revision itself produced a benefit.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: Well calibrated: “it does not establish that ‘AI-assisted’ scheduling causally reduces DSM exposure in general” and “treat the number as a single reproducible data point.”
It distinguishes arithmetic reproducibility from causal identification and explicitly states what remains unknown, including whether the revision would work on the 28-May wind trace.
The proposed backtest is a concrete decision-changing measurement rather than a generic request for more data.

dimensions.name: Decision/action quality
citations: The recommendation to “continue the pilot as a measurement exercise” while not expanding or commercially relying on 31.6% appropriately preserves possible value without overclaiming.
The proposed backtest of the same revision logic on 28-May is a useful discriminating test.
The action would be stronger if it first reported the observed 29-May same-day base-versus-submitted result and then specified matched-day or randomized operational validation.

dimensions.name: Conclusion fit
citations: The conclusion correctly distinguishes “pilot day performed better” from proof that the pilot “caused 31.6% reduction,” directly addressing the different-day comparison.
It appropriately retains a possible operational benefit rather than concluding the method is worthless.

It does not preserve the smaller same-day benefit visible from comparing base_schedule_mw with submitted_schedule_mw on 29-May, so it is directionally right but incomplete relative to the strongest supported conclusion.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: “Curtailment = 0 on both days, ruling out curtailment as a confound” is too broad; it rules out curtailment as a measured factor but does not resolve other day-specific confounding.

“The 12 revised blocks ... directly lowering the applicable Rs/kWh rate” is supported for the cited blocks and rate bands, but the submission does not show the aggregate same-day penalty difference against the unrevised 29-May base schedule.

The inference that a successful 28-May backtest would establish that the method effect is separable from weather is too strong: one additional retrospective day would improve evidence but would not fully identify causality.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The 29-May revision likely produced a smaller but real same-day improvement when submitted_schedule_mw is compared with base_schedule_mw on the same actual wind trace. Thus, the evidence may support limited value from the revision while not supporting the headline 31.6% causal claim, which is based on comparing different days.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Compute and report the 29-May same-day counterfactual directly: recompute DSM penalty and absolute generation gap using base_schedule_mw versus submitted_schedule_mw while holding 29-May actual generation, rates, and conditions fixed; then compare that result with the cross-day 31.6% figure.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "28-May penalty = Rs 662,444; 29-May penalty = Rs 453,086; (662,444−453,086)/662,444 = 31.6% exactly" tied to "dispatch_blocks.csv, dsm_penalty_rs summed per date"
"Only 12 of 96 blocks on 29-May carry schedule_source = \"pilot_revision\"" tied to "dispatch_blocks.csv, schedule_source column"
"The 12 revised blocks fall in the 13:00-15:45 stow window" tied to "dispatch_blocks.csv + DSM_Commercial_Extract.pdf deviation-band table"

dimensions.name: Reasoning and hypothesis testing
citations: "Rejected: \"The broker filed the wrong tariff code.\""
"Rejected: \"This is a duty-revenue-impacting error.\""
"if Switzerland has since adopted an 8-digit-equivalent code closer to 90211090, that would change this from \"expected encoding difference\" to \"stale local reference\""

dimensions.name: Calibration
citations: "I cannot see the Swiss customs \"Tares\" ruling database or a product-specific classification ruling for P1001"
"if Switzerland has since adopted an 8-digit-equivalent code closer to 90211090, that would change this"
"a low-cost verification, not an escalation"

dimensions.name: Process and system understanding
citations: "The mismatch ... is a cross-schema encoding artefact, not a classification disagreement"
"the declaration used Switzerland's local Swiss tariff code ... while Helios stores an EU-style CN8/US-migration code"
"flag Helios's product master as needing an origin-system/nomenclature tag so future automated comparisons stop flagging cross-schema code differences as mismatches"

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: "Do not escalate as a declaration error"
"Route this to the Swiss country trade owner to confirm whether 90211000 remains the current Tares-approved code for P1001"
"a low-cost verification, not an escalation"

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: The characterization of Helios 90211090 as an "EU-style CN8/US-migration code" and the assertion that its schema is "explicitly not designed to compare against Swiss codes" are plausible but are not directly demonstrated by the evidence table beyond the quoted tariff-matrix statement that "matching strings across jurisdictions is not expected."

The claim that the two codes produce "no revenue effect" depends on the asserted 0.0% duty rate and the absence of a Swiss-specific Helios rate; those underlying records are not identified separately in the evidence table.

The conclusion that the 12 revised blocks "directly" lowered the applicable rate would be stronger with block-level rate calculations or a counterfactual showing the avoided penalty, rather than only the stated deviation-band movement.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The Swiss local reference may be stale, or the product may have a different legally applicable classification under a current product-specific Tares ruling; alternatively, Helios's code could itself be erroneous rather than merely a cross-schema representation. The submission appropriately preserves the first alternative but does not independently test the latter two.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Attach the current Tares/product-specific classification evidence and a block-level reconciliation of the 12 pilot-revision blocks, including the applicable rate before and after revision, to substantiate both the benign-code conclusion and the claimed penalty mechanism.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: The submission identifies the invoice and chat-log files for the distinction between “manufacturing country” and preferential origin.
It cites “supplier_origin_register.csv (Row 3)” and “supplier_origin_register.csv (Row 8)” for the supplier records and “image_f4ef21.png (search result)” for the failed search.

It appropriately identifies missing evidence: “A master data mapping or confirmation that the seller ‘Asterion Manufacturing Services’ ... explicitly corresponds to supplier ID SUP-01” and “The actual supplier declaration document SD-SUP-01-P1006-2025 ... to verify the specific preference rules applied.”

dimensions.name: Reasoning and hypothesis testing
citations: The submission explicitly rejects approval based only on the invoice: “The preference claim should be approved based on the commercial invoice: Rejected.”
It tests the absence hypothesis by distinguishing the failed SUP-02 search from the register record: “No valid supplier declaration exists for this product: Rejected.”
However, it does not fully test whether the SUP-01 record applies to this transaction, product rules, or shipper beyond acknowledging that mapping is missing.

dimensions.name: Calibration
citations: The conclusion is appropriately conditional: “The preferential-origin claim is not currently supported by the provided case packet.”

It identifies important uncertainty: “A master data mapping or confirmation ... explicitly corresponds to supplier ID SUP-01” and requests “The actual supplier declaration document ... to verify the specific preference rules applied.”

Calibration is weakened by stating that “valid supporting documentation likely exists” and that “A valid supplier declaration ... currently exists,” although the cited register appears to establish a record or metadata entry rather than the underlying declaration document.

dimensions.name: Process and system understanding
citations: The submission gives a plausible data-lineage explanation: “The system's failure to find supporting documentation in ClearView appears to be caused by querying the wrong supplier ID (SUP-02) instead of the supplier associated with US-origin goods (SUP-01).”

It recognizes the distinction between ERP data and preference evidence, quoting that ERP manufacturing-country data “was never designed to prove preference” and that “a formal supplier declaration is required to clear a claim.”
The mechanism remains partly unverified because the submission itself says mapping the seller to SUP-01 is missing.

dimensions.name: Decision safety
citations: The submission gives a cautious hold instruction: “Do not clear the claim until the correct document is linked.”

Its proposed action is proportionate and reversible: “Contact Procurement Shared Services ... to retrieve the supplier declaration document,” then “Verify that this document covers the shipper ... and manually link it to the ClearView packet.”
It avoids declaring fraud or definitively invalidating the claim, while requiring supplier evidence before clearance.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: “Valid supporting documentation likely exists” is speculative; the evidence cited shows a register entry, not that the underlying supplier declaration is present or valid for this transaction.

“A valid supplier declaration for US-origin P1006 currently exists in the register” overstates what a register row establishes. It supports that a declaration record is listed, but not the contents, authenticity, applicability, or current availability of the document.

“The supplier associated with US-origin goods (SUP-01)” and the claim that SUP-02 was definitively the wrong supplier remain unconfirmed because the submission identifies the missing mapping between “Asterion Manufacturing Services” and SUP-01.

The statement that the invoice is “legally insufficient” is directionally supported by the cited customs-team note, but the submission does not provide the specific legal rule or jurisdictional basis.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The SUP-01 register record may be unrelated to the shipment: the seller could map to another supplier ID, the declaration may not cover the relevant transaction or preference rule, or the register may contain only a historical/metadata record. The SUP-02 search failure therefore does not by itself establish that ClearView queried the wrong supplier or that the claim is supportable.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Verify the master-data mapping and retrieve the actual SD-SUP-01-P1006-2025 document before characterizing it as valid or concluding that the ClearView search used the wrong supplier.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "185 out of 262 records (70.6%) have a qcore_release_ts of exactly 02:10:00"; "batch_release.csv, source_freshness.csv" — specific and relevant field-level evidence, though the submission does not quote the underlying rows or fully reconcile the snapshot timing.

"The SLA defines the target as '24 hours from required evidence available to disposition'"; "QL-204 (Service target), batch_release.csv" — directly links the conclusion to the SOP and observed interval.

dimensions.name: Causal / investigative reasoning
citations: "The disposition timestamp is heavily polluted by an ETL batch artifact" and "destroying intra-day resolution" — the concentration supports a timestamp/interface artifact, but does not by itself establish that the value is an overwrite rather than a legitimate release or interface commit.

"Operations is measuring the wrong interval" — the receipt-to-release comparison is relevant, but the evidence does not establish that Operations actually uses receipt_ts or quantify the required-evidence-to-release interval.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: The table labels the timestamp, latency, and milestone conclusions "High" confidence, although the event/decision timestamp definition and coherent snapshot status remain unresolved.

"accurate daily KPI reporting [is] impossible without correction" and "a live 24-hour KPI dashboard is structurally impossible" — these are stronger than the evidence supports; stale extracts may prevent current-state monitoring but do not necessarily prevent lagged measurement or retrospective KPI reporting.

dimensions.name: Decision usefulness / reframing
citations: "Do not build the dashboard yet" — appropriately reframes the task around KPI validity before implementation.

"Review the enterprise data catalog ... to determine if a true transactional event timestamp exists" — a useful, reversible safeguard against optimizing a measurement artifact, although the recommendation should also define a temporary lagged/reporting use case and acceptance criteria.

dimensions.name: Disconfirmation and rejected hypotheses
citations: "Operations' 'day and a half' estimate is an accurate reflection of standard performance: Rejected" — correctly uses the SOP's clock-start and exception rules, but does not test the actual required-evidence timestamp.

"The 02:10:00 release times represent an automated nightly batch release: Rejected" — the evidence supports a batch/interface-timing explanation but does not distinguish a genuine automated release process from an enterprise reporting overwrite; the alternative is rejected too confidently.

dimensions.name: Questioning / next evidence
citations: "Review the enterprise data catalog ... if a true transactional event timestamp exists" — this is a high-value, targeted request that directly discriminates process timing from interface timing.

"Confirmation from data engineering on whether LabTrack can be upgraded from a 48-hour extract to an intra-day feed" — relevant, but less immediate and not necessarily the smallest next test compared with obtaining event-log samples and timestamp semantics.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: That the 02:10:00 values are definitively an ETL overwrite rather than interface commit or a legitimate automated release timestamp.
That Operations is measuring from receipt_ts; the dataset shows that interval, but does not prove the operational KPI definition.
That a 48-hour LabTrack extract makes accurate daily KPI reporting or any 24-hour KPI monitoring structurally impossible; it primarily creates reporting lag and snapshot-alignment risk.
That the data pipelines make KPI reporting impossible without correction, rather than making the current KPI definition and freshness unsuitable for an operational dashboard.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The apparent long cycle may reflect a mixture of real workflow time, waiting for required evidence, and delayed enterprise/interface commits. The 02:10 concentration may be a genuine batch/interface timestamp rather than a corrupted overwrite, while the non-coherent QCore and LabTrack extracts make end-to-end joins and current-state claims unreliable. A valid lagged retrospective KPI might still be possible after defining event semantics and aligning snapshots.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Obtain a small event-log sample for the same cases containing required-evidence-available, disposition-decision, QCore interface-commit, and extract/snapshot timestamps, then reconcile it to source freshness. This would discriminate workflow delay from timestamp artifact and establish whether a lagged or operational 24-hour KPI is feasible before pursuing pipeline upgrades.

dimensions.name: Evidence traceability
citations: "MaintStar-global snapshot is from 2026-06-26T00:00:00, while the part requests were generated in July (PR-2607xx)." — precise source and timing evidence, though not tied to row-level inventory fields.

"$108,561 of the $152,558 requested value fails due to zero cross-site stock, wrong revision, wrong UOM, or all existing stock being reserved for critical assets." — cites the relevant files, but does not show the specific rows or restriction values supporting each grouped amount.
"Global available quantity can lag a local reservation" from the Leon Dube email — useful independent corroboration of the freshness concern.

dimensions.name: Causal / investigative reasoning
citations: "All identified candidate matches must be verified on live local CMMS screens before canceling external purchase requests." — correctly separates candidate retrieval from transfer authorization.
"Requests for 'servo drv 2.2kW' ... can be fulfilled by Riverbend or Meridian: Rejected ... reserved for a critical asset (True)." — tests a plausible alternative against the restrictions file.

The reasoning identifies both stale availability and reservation/qualification constraints, but does not demonstrate manufacturer-part-number, revision, UOM, or catalog-equivalence checks for each candidate.

dimensions.name: Calibration and uncertainty
citations: "$0 is actionable now, $43,997 needs engineering/local check" — appropriately treats stale inventory as preventing immediate authorization.
"Global inventory data is over a month old" and "local check is still mandatory" — uncertainty is tied to a specific timestamp and operational consequence.

The "High" confidence assigned to "$108,561 ... has no valid transfer option" is too strong when the underlying availability extract is stale and the submission does not distinguish current non-transferability from non-transferability in the snapshot.

dimensions.name: Decision usefulness / reframing
citations: "All identified candidate matches must be verified on live local CMMS screens before canceling external purchase requests." — gives a concrete safeguard against erroneous cancellation or transfer.

"If local planners can confirm the physical stock is present and unreserved in real-time, those specific transfers would become actionable." — proposes a reversible next step with a clear decision criterion.
The recommendation would be stronger if it explicitly required manufacturer part number, revision, UOM, qualification, requested quantity, and reservation confirmation before approving a transfer.

dimensions.name: Disconfirmation and rejected hypotheses
citations: "Matches with 'QUALIFIED_COMMON' site qualification are actionable now: Rejected" — considers and rejects a plausible operational interpretation using the freshness warning.
"Requests for 'servo drv 2.2kW' ... can be fulfilled ... Rejected" — tests the apparent stock against the critical-asset reservation flag.

It does not actively test the strongest competing explanation for the remaining candidates: semantic similarity may not establish catalog equivalence or transferability, particularly where manufacturer part number, revision, or UOM differ.

dimensions.name: Questioning / next evidence
citations: "I would request a live pull from the local MaintStar screens ... for the specific candidate matches listed above." — asks for targeted, high-value evidence rather than generic additional data.
"If local planners can confirm the physical stock is present and unreserved in real-time, those specific transfers would become actionable." — explains the decision impact of the requested evidence.
The request should also specify the exact identity and control fields to retrieve, especially manufacturer part number, revision, UOM, qualification, requested quantity, and reservation status.

unsupported_or_overstated_claims: "$0 is actionable now" is operationally conservative, but the submission does not establish whether any stock has independently current local confirmation; stale global data alone means unknown, not necessarily zero.

"71.2% of requested value has no valid transfer option" and the associated High confidence overstate what can be concluded from an old inventory snapshot. The claim should be bounded as no valid option in the supplied snapshot pending current verification.

The candidate table presents grouped request-to-stock matches without row-level manufacturer part number, revision, UOM, qualification, quantity, or reservation evidence, so semantic matches may be mistaken for catalog-equivalent transfer options.
per_question.strongest_alternative_interpretation: The stale global extract makes immediate transfer authorization unsafe, but it does not prove that all $43,997 of candidate value requires engineering review or that $108,561 is permanently non-transferable. Some candidates may be operationally transferable after a live local check, while others may fail because semantic similarity does not establish manufacturer-part-number and revision equivalence.
per_question.single_most_valuable_next_improvement: Obtain a targeted, current local MaintStar reconciliation for each candidate, keyed by manufacturer part number and including revision, UOM, requested and available quantity, site qualification, and reservation/criticality status; use it to reclassify candidate value into confirmed actionable, engineering review, and non-transferable value before canceling requests.
